questions.question: Explain how different ideas about land contributed to conflict at the Cape.
questions.expected_answer: Khoikhoi held land in common, with clans having seasonal rights to grazing and water, not saleable by individuals; San had shared hunting and gathering territories. Colonists saw land as private property that could be granted by the VOC, fenced, registered and sold, and regarded unploughed land as empty. So Khoikhoi permission to graze temporarily was treated by colonists as permanent transfer, causing disputes and war.

questions.question: Describe the different ways in which the Khoikhoi and San were dispossessed.
questions.expected_answer: Settlement on Khoikhoi grazing land from 1657 without consent; wars (1659-60 led by Doman; 1673-77 against Gonnema's Cochoqua) and land claimed by conquest; loss of cattle through unequal trade and raids; smallpox epidemics (1713, 1755, 1767); trekboer expansion through loan farms; commandos killing San and capturing children; colonial law not recognising indigenous ownership, and later the Caledon Code (1809).

questions.question: What were the consequences of dispossession for the indigenous population, and why do they matter today?
questions.expected_answer: Loss of political independence (chiefdoms broke up); loss of livelihood (land and cattle) so many became farm labourers, soldiers or mission residents; unfree labour (debt, indenture, passes); large population losses from war, disease and violence; destruction of San communities and loss of languages (e.g. !Xam) and culture; some moved north (Kora, Griqua, Nama). Today: restitution only covers losses after 19 June 1913, so most Khoi and San losses are excluded; some progress (Khomani San claim 1999; Traditional and Khoi-San Leadership Act 2019); land remains debated.
